questions.topicName: Regulation, KYC, ethics and investor remedies
questions.learningObjective: Know what happens when a client takes a complaint to CIRO arbitration instead of court. (Volume 1 Ch3 LO3).
questions.questionText: Priya is a retail client of an investment dealer that is a CIRO member. She believes unsuitable recommendations cost her $350,000. She raised the complaint with the firm first and is not satisfied with its answer, so she asks to use CIRO's arbitration program. Assume the program works as the course text describes, with a maximum claim of $500,000. Which statement is correct?
options: OBSI's recommendation is binding on the firm, so arbitration is unnecessary.
The arbitrator can only make a non-binding recommendation, so Priya can still sue the firm over the same claim afterwards.
The dealer must take part in the arbitration, and the arbitrator's decision is binding on both sides.
The dealer may decline arbitration because participation is voluntary for member firms.
questions.explanation: Under the program described in the course text, once a client who has already tried to settle with the firm chooses arbitration within the claim limit ($350,000 is below $500,000), the dealer is required to participate and the award is final and binding. Note: Limit of $500,000 and dealer-must-participate rule as stated in the 2025 course text and on the CIRO page dated 2025-07-23. CIRO has published a proposal (21 Feb 2025) to change the arbitration program, which had not been confirmed as adopted at the research date. Re-check before relying on the dollar limit. Research date: 15 Nov 2026.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong. OBSI is a separate route and its recommendations are not binding on the firm, which is why some clients choose arbitration.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong. The arbitration award is binding, and the client gives up the right to take the same claim to court. A non-binding recommendation describes the ombudsman route, not arbitration.
optionAnalysis.C: Under the program described in the course text, once a client who has already tried to settle with the firm chooses arbitration within the claim limit ($350,000 is below $500,000), the dealer is required to participate and the award is final and binding.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong. The dealer cannot refuse when a qualifying client elects arbitration; participation is mandatory for the firm (the client's choice triggers it).

questions.topicName: Regulation, KYC, ethics and investor remedies
questions.learningObjective: Describe what OBSI is and how binding its recommendations are. (Volume 1 Ch3 LO3).
questions.questionText: A client wants an independent review of a complaint about her advisor and is considering the Ombudsman for Banking Services and Investments (OBSI). Assume OBSI works as described in the course text and in its consumer FAQs at the research date. Which statement about OBSI is correct?
options: OBSI is a government regulator that can fine advisors and suspend their registration.
OBSI's decisions are legally binding and enforced through court if the firm refuses.
OBSI is a department within the dealer's compliance team that handles complaints after internal escalation.
OBSI is independent of the securities industry; its recommendations are not binding, but a firm that refuses to follow one can be publicly identified.
questions.explanation: This matches the course text and OBSI's own FAQs: independence, non-binding recommendations, and public reporting of firms that refuse. Note: OBSI recommendations are not binding at the research date. A CSA proposal to give OBSI binding authority was still a proposal and was not treated as in force. Re-check if that framework is adopted. Research date: 15 Nov 2026.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong. OBSI is not a regulator and has no power to discipline, fine or suspend advisors; discipline is for regulators such as CIRO.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong. OBSI cannot compel a firm to pay. The consequence of refusal is public naming, not a court-enforced order.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong. OBSI is independent of the firms it reviews; it is not part of any dealer's compliance function.
optionAnalysis.D: This matches the course text and OBSI's own FAQs: independence, non-binding recommendations, and public reporting of firms that refuse.

questions.topicName: Regulation, KYC, ethics and investor remedies
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a fictitious trade that creates a false picture of market activity. (Volume 1 Ch3 LO4).
questions.questionText: One person controls Account A and Account B. Over three days he sells 5,000 shares of a thinly traded stock from Account A to Account B, each day at a slightly higher price. The real owner of the shares never changes. Other investors see the rising price and volume and start buying. Which practice does this best illustrate?
options: A fictitious trade with no change in beneficial ownership, used to create a false appearance of active trading.
questions.explanation: Moving shares between accounts of the same beneficial owner at rising prices is the textbook example of a fictitious trade intended to mislead the public.

optionAnalysis.A: Moving shares between accounts of the same beneficial owner at rising prices is the textbook example of a fictitious trade intended to mislead the public.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong. Front running means trading for one's own account before executing the same trade for a client. No client order is involved here.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong. Arbitrage profits from price differences between markets or instruments, with real transfers of ownership. Here nothing real changes hands.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong. Insider trading is trading on undisclosed material information. The scenario describes artificial activity, not use of inside information.

questions.questionText: Over one year Canada buys more goods and services from the rest of the world than it sells, producing a current account deficit of $30 billion. Ignoring statistical discrepancies, what must the capital and financial account show?

optionAnalysis.A: The balance of payments must balance: a current account deficit is financed by an equal net inflow in the capital and financial account (called the financial account plus capital account in newer Statistics Canada tables).

questions.questionText: A Canadian firm sells a part for a fixed price of C$2,000. A U.S. customer pays in U.S. dollars at the prevailing rate. The exchange rate moves from US$0.72 to US$0.65 per C$1, and the firm keeps its Canadian-dollar price unchanged. What is the new U.S.-dollar price, and what is the effect on the firm's competitiveness?
options: US$3,077; the part is more expensive for the U.S. buyer, so the firm is less competitive.
US$1,440; the price is unchanged, so competitiveness is unchanged.

questions.questionText: An economy's real GDP is $1,200 billion in Year 1, produced with 24.0 billion hours worked. In Year 2 real GDP is $1,272 billion, produced with 24.6 billion hours worked. Using output per hour worked as the measure of productivity, by about how much did productivity grow (to the nearest 0.1%)?
questions.explanation: Productivity rose from $50.00 to $51.71 of real output per hour, up 3.4%. Real GDP grew 6.0%, but 2.5% worth of that came from more hours. Working: Year 1: 1,200 / 24.0 = $50.00 per hour. Year 2: 1,272 / 24.6 = $51.71 per hour. Growth = 51.71 / 50.00 - 1 = 3.4%. (Check: 1.060 / 1.025 = 1.0341.) optionAnalysis.A: Productivity rose from $50.00 to $51.71 of real output per hour, up 3.4%. Real GDP grew 6.0%, but 2.5% worth of that came from more hours.

optionAnalysis.C: Wrong. This is growth in real GDP. It includes the effect of more hours worked, which is not a productivity gain.

questions.questionText: Marc buys a $10,000 five-year index-linked GIC with a 60% participation rate. Over the term the linked index rises 35%. The GIC guarantees return of the initial investment at maturity. What is the value of the GIC at maturity, ignoring tax and fees?
questions.explanation: Gain = 60% x 35% = 21.0% of $10,000 = $2,100; total $12,100. Working: Index gain 35% x participation 60% = 21.0%. $10,000 x 0.21 = $2,100. Value = $10,000 + $2,100 = $12,100. questions.learningObjective: Use the expectations theory to find the one-year rate the market implies for next year. (Volume 1 Ch7 LO2).
questions.questionText: Government bond yields are 2.5% for one year and 4.5% for two years (annual compounding). Under the expectations theory, which one-year rate one year from now would make a two-year bond and two consecutive one-year bonds equally attractive, and what does the curve shape say about expected rates? Round to the nearest 0.1%.
options: About 4.5%; the curve indicates rates are expected to stay flat.
About 2.0%; the curve indicates rates are expected to fall.
About 3.5%; the curve indicates rates are expected to fall.
About 6.5%; the upward-sloping curve indicates the market expects rates to rise.
questions.explanation: (1.045)^2 = 1.092025; divide by 1.025 = 1.06539; subtract 1 = 6.54%, or 6.5% to one decimal. Working: (1 + 0.045)^2 = (1 + 0.025) x (1 + r). 1.045^2 = 1.092025. 1.092025 / 1.025 = 1.06539. r = 0.06539 = 6.54%, about 6.5%. Rate rises from 2.5% to ~6.5%, so the market expects higher rates. Note: Annual compounding; textbook method (pure expectations theory, no liquidity premium). Research date: 15 Nov 2026.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong. 4.5% is just the two-year rate. A year-two rate equal to it would not reproduce the two-year return, and an upward slope is not flat.
optionAnalysis.B: Wrong. 2.0% is the difference between the two rates and has no basis in the compounding equation.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong. 3.5% is the simple average of the two quoted rates, which ignores the one-year rate already locked in; an upward slope does not signal falling rates.

questions.questionText: A TSX-listed company declares a dividend with a record date of Monday, December 14, 2026. Assume standard T+1 settlement for equities and no holidays in the period. What is the last trading day on which a buyer is entitled to the dividend?
questions.explanation: Under T+1 the ex-dividend date equals the record date (Monday Dec 14). A trade on Friday Dec 11 settles on Monday Dec 14, so the buyer is on the register on the record date. Monday's trade would settle Tuesday, too late. Working: T+1: ex-date = record date = Mon 14 Dec. Last cum-dividend trade is the previous business day: Fri 11 Dec (settles Mon 14 Dec). Note: T+1 equity settlement in effect since 27 May 2024; ex-date same as record date for regular dividends. Special rules (large stock dividends, due bills) not covered. Research date: 15 Nov 2026.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong. Sunday is not a business day, so no trading takes place.
optionAnalysis.B: Under T+1 the ex-dividend date equals the record date (Monday Dec 14). A trade on Friday Dec 11 settles on Monday Dec 14, so the buyer is on the register on the record date. Monday's trade would settle Tuesday, too late.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong. This applies the old T+2 rule, where the last cum-dividend day was two business days before the record date. Under T+1, Friday still qualifies.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong. Monday is the ex-dividend date; a buyer on Monday settles Tuesday, after the record date, and does not receive the dividend.

questions.learningObjective: Compare how a price-weighted average and a value-weighted index react to the same price move. (Volume 1 Ch8 LO5).
questions.questionText: Three stocks make up a small market: X trades at $100 with 1,000,000 shares outstanding, Y at $40 with 5,000,000 shares, and Z at $10 with 20,000,000 shares. A price-weighted average divides the sum of prices by 3, and a value-weighted index tracks total market capitalization. If X falls 10% and the other two are unchanged, what are the percentage changes in the price-weighted average and in the value-weighted index?
options: Both change by -10%, because X fell 10%.
questions.explanation: Price-weighted: ($90+$40+$10)/3 = $46.67 vs $50.00 = -6.67%. Value-weighted: market cap falls from $500M to $490M = -2.0%. Working: Price-weighted before: (100+40+10)/3 = 50.00. After: (90+40+10)/3 = 46.67. Change = -6.67%. Market cap before: 100M + 200M + 200M = 500M. After: 90M + 200M + 200M = 490M. Change = -10/500 = -2.0%. Note: No divisor adjustments; no dividends. Research date: 15 Nov 2026.

optionAnalysis.A: Wrong. The two results are swapped. X has the highest price, which gives it a large weight in the price-weighted average, but only a 20% share of total market value.
optionAnalysis.B: Price-weighted: ($90+$40+$10)/3 = $46.67 vs $50.00 = -6.67%. Value-weighted: market cap falls from $500M to $490M = -2.0%.
optionAnalysis.C: Wrong. -0.67% is what the price-weighted average would show if the $10 stock Z fell 10%, not X.
optionAnalysis.D: Wrong. Only X fell; the other stocks dilute the effect in both measures.
